note.explanation: Metals can lose electrons and become positive ions. How easily they lose electrons is linked to how reactive they are.
examples: Sodium and potassium lose electrons easily, so they are highly electropositive and react vigorously.
Magnesium and calcium lose their outer electrons less easily, so they are less electropositive than sodium and potassium.
note.simple: Electropositive metals give away electrons. Metals that give them away easily are more reactive.
note.checkQuestion: What type of elements gain electrons easily?
note.title: Electropositive Character of Metals
steps: A metal loses one or more electrons.
Losing electrons forms a positive ion called a cation.
A metal that loses electrons easily is more reactive.
note.answer: Metals generally have a tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions called cations. This property is called the electropositive character of metals.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean if a metal is highly electropositive?
rationales: Correct: highly electropositive metals lose electrons easily.
Incorrect: gaining electrons is not the property described for metals in this section.
Incorrect: sharing electrons does not define electropositive character.
Incorrect: metals can form positive ions by losing electrons.

mcqs.stem: What positive ions form when metals lose electrons?
rationales: Correct: positive ions formed by losing electrons are called cations.
Incorrect: anions are negative ions, not positive ions.
Incorrect: an atom that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
Incorrect: the section names these positive ions cations.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is identified in the section as an alkali metal that is highly electropositive?
rationales: Correct: sodium is named as a highly electropositive alkali metal.
Incorrect: magnesium is an alkaline earth metal and is less electropositive than alkali metals.
Incorrect: calcium is an alkaline earth metal and is less electropositive than alkali metals.
Incorrect: aluminium is highly electropositive, but it is not an alkali metal.

options: They lose their outer electrons less easily
mcqs.stem: Why are alkaline earth metals such as magnesium and calcium less electropositive than alkali metals?
rationales: Correct: the section says they lose their outer electrons less easily.
Incorrect: the section compares how easily they lose electrons, not how easily they gain them.
Incorrect: the section says their reactions towards water are less vigorous, not that they cannot react.
Incorrect: magnesium and calcium are metals.

options: They are highly electropositive and lose electrons easily
They gain electrons to form negative ions
They are less reactive than alkaline earth metals
They do not react with halogens
mcqs.stem: According to the section, why do sodium and potassium react very easily?
rationales: Correct: they are highly electropositive and lose electrons easily.
Incorrect: the section describes these metals as losing electrons, not gaining them.
Incorrect: the section describes alkali metals as highly reactive compared with alkaline earth metals.
Incorrect: the section says they react with halogens.

options: It reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen
It is an alkaline earth metal
It gains electrons easily to form anions
mcqs.stem: Which statement about aluminium agrees with the section?
rationales: Correct: the section says aluminium reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen.
Incorrect: aluminium is not identified as an alkaline earth metal.
Incorrect: the section specifically describes its reaction with mineral acids.
Incorrect: aluminium is described as a highly electropositive metal, not as forming anions by gaining electrons.

written.text: What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?
written.finalAnswer: Metals lose their outer electrons easily, and non-metals gain electrons easily.

rubric.why: The answer must also identify the elements that readily gain electrons.
rubric.description: Gives the correct final answer for the elements that gain electrons.
rubric.how: State that non-metals gain electrons easily.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask which types of elements lose or gain electrons; name metals and non-metals clearly.
For a question on electropositive character, state that metals lose electrons to form positive ions called cations.
When comparing metals, mention that alkali metals lose electrons more easily than alkaline earth metals, so they are more reactive.
For full marks, connect the ease of losing electrons with reactivity and use the examples given in your textbook.

steps.text: Sodium and potassium are highly electropositive elements.

steps.why: Electropositive metals lose electrons easily, which the section links with greater reactivity.
steps.text: They lose electrons easily and thus undergo reactions very easily.

steps.why: This gives examples of the reactions that show their high reactivity.
steps.text: They react vigorously with water and halogens, and they also react with acids to give salts and hydrogen.

example.question: Why do sodium and potassium undergo reactions very easily?
example.answer: Sodium and potassium are highly electropositive, so they lose electrons easily and react very easily.

explain.title: What electropositive character means
explain.body: Metals generally have a tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions called cations. This property is called the electropositive character of metals.

explain.title: Electropositive character and reactivity
explain.body: This property is also related to the reactivity of the metals. Metals which lose electron or electrons easily are considered more reactive.

explain.title: Alkali metals
explain.body: Alkali metals (Na, K) are highly electropositive elements and thus they undergo reactions very easily. Sodium and potassium react vigorously with water and halogens to give their respective hydroxides and halides. They also react with acids to give salts and hydrogen.

explain.title: Alkaline earth metals
explain.body: Alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca), on the other hand, lose their outer electrons less easily and thus they are less electropositive than alkali metals. Their reactions towards water and halogens are also less vigorous.

explain.title: Aluminium
explain.body: Aluminum is also highly electropositive metal. It reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen.

mistakes: Do not say metals gain electrons in this section; they lose electrons to form positive cations.
Do not confuse cations with anions: cations are positive ions.
Do not describe alkaline earth metals as more electropositive than alkali metals; they lose their outer electrons less easily.
When asked why a metal is more reactive, explain the link to how easily it loses electrons.
